summary:
Louisiana has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, or public accommodations. As of 12 October 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scores the state's gender-identity policy at -8.75/25, with recourse limited to federal EEOC processes and the June 2020 Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County for employment claims only. Local ordinances provide partial cover: New Orleans and Shreveport prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Lake Charles and Jefferson Parish extend protection only to public employees.

The 1997 state hate-crime statute, which provides penalty enhancements, covers sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation but does not include gender identity. Hate crimes motivated by gender identity therefore fall to federal prosecution under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009.

Physical safety data for Louisiana is severe. A July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams Institute data reports Louisiana with the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state, 24.7 per 100,000 per year (19 recorded killings), against 23.5 for the state ranked safest on this measure, drawn from a base of 428 US victims recorded 2008–2025. The source cautions that every figure is an undercount floor and that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, with the worst-law states holding the highest rate.

Trans-specific violence has been documented with direct legal consequences. In August 2026 a mob attacked trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton over restroom use; Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who sustained a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested. Rush was denied hospital care, jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. Reporting on 5 August 2026 notes the plea deal was not signed and that the Sheriff's Office confirmed no other arrests that day; the same municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances.

Trans people in state custody face documented harm. Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024. This was at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person killed in the United States in 2024 that the Human Rights Campaign had learned of, and the fifth in April alone; such deaths are systematically under- or mis-reported.

Identity documents in Louisiana are changed only through surgery. A driver's licence gender marker may be changed on submission of a physician-signed statement confirming successful sex reassignment surgery. A new birth certificate requires a certified court order confirming surgical gender change, proof of diagnosis as transsexual or pseudo-hermaphrodite, and evidence of anatomical change.

Transition-related healthcare for minors is banned. In July 2023 the Legislature overrode the Governor's June 2023 veto to prohibit puberty blockers, hormones, and surgeries for minors, formally effective 1 January 2024. Surgery, puberty blockers, hormone replacement therapy and other transition-related care are excluded from health insurance and state Medicaid coverage.

Facilities and sport rules restrict trans participation. In June 2022 Louisiana banned transgender girls from sports in public schools, passed with more than two-thirds support in both chambers after a similar 2021 bill (House 77-17, Senate 29-6) was vetoed and the override failed by two votes. The Benton incident above shows restroom restrictions being enforced by mob violence and subsequently codified in municipal ordinance.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by the 2003 Lawrence v. Texas ruling and a 2005 Fifth Circuit decision, though an unenforceable sodomy law carrying up to five years imprisonment, a $2,000 fine and sex-offender registration remains on the books after repeal failed 66-27 in April 2014. Same-sex marriage has been recognised since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with compliance confirmed two days later; married same-sex couples are entitled to full joint adoption and parental rights following Costanza v. Caldwell of 22 September 2014. A June 2017 domestic-violence amendment removed opposite-sex language, ensuring identical treatment irrespective of sexual orientation where same-sex offenders previously received lesser sentences. Louisiana also maintains a no-promo-homo law barring sex education classes from discussing male or female homosexual activity.
tangentialFactors:
The Needle analysis cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety: the state with the highest per-capita trans killing rate is not the state with the worst legal framework, and the worst-law states hold the highest rate. Raw counts and per-capita rates should be read against the 428-victim national base for 2008–2025, itself an undercount floor.

Louisiana's document-change regime requiring surgery is stricter than many states, which may affect how a trans visitor's home-state or federal documents align with Louisiana practice if a local stop involves document checking.

Local ordinances in New Orleans and Shreveport provide gender-identity protections absent at state level, so exposure varies materially by city within Louisiana.
localsOnly:
Residents face a state-level gap in gender-identity protections: no state nondiscrimination law covers employment, housing, or public accommodations, leaving only federal EEOC and Bostock-based court recourse for employment, and no state remedy for housing, health care, education, credit or public accommodations. Executive orders barring sexual-orientation discrimination in state employment (1992, 2004, 2016) all lapsed, expired or were struck down, with the litigation resolved on appeal in March 2018.

Gender-marker changes on a Louisiana driver's licence require a physician-signed statement confirming successful sex reassignment surgery. A new birth certificate requires a certified court order confirming surgical gender change, proof of diagnosis as transsexual or pseudo-hermaphrodite, and anatomical change.

Transition-related care for minors has been banned since 1 January 2024 following the July 2023 veto override; surgery, puberty blockers, hormone replacement therapy and other transition-related healthcare are excluded from health insurance and state Medicaid coverage.

Transgender girls are barred from public-school sports under the June 2022 law. Gender-identity-based hate crimes receive no state penalty enhancement, relying on federal prosecution.

Residents in New Orleans and Shreveport have local gender-identity protections in employment, housing and public accommodations; residents of Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Lake Charles and Jefferson Parish are protected only as public employees.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that Louisiana's per-capita trans killing rate is the highest of any state rests on a July 2026 secondary analysis of TGEU/Williams data; the underlying methodology for the 24.7 per 100,000 figure and the 19 recorded killings is not independently verifiable from the source inventory and should be treated as reported rather than audited.

The plea disposition in the Benton case (Rush and Sanders charged with disturbing the peace) is unresolved in the sources: one report notes the plea deal was not signed, and no later outcome is available.

Whether the 1997 hate-crime statute has ever been applied through federal prosecution for a gender-identity-motivated crime in Louisiana is not sourced here.

Two bills related to the 2023 minor-care ban were described as awaiting legislative action as of the source's writing; their current status is unresolved.

The unenforceable sodomy statute remains on the books but is treated as non-operative following Lawrence v. Texas and the 2005 Fifth Circuit ruling; whether any enforcement attempt has occurred is not sourced.
